core: Cognitivism as the mid-century turn from studying behavior alone to studying the internal processing between input and response
The information-processing model: sensory registers, a limited short-term store or working memory, and a long-term store, linked by control processes such as attention and rehearsal
Capacity: Miller's seven-plus-or-minus-two chunk claim and its revision to roughly three to four chunks under conditions that block rehearsal and grouping
Chunking, and the fact that chunk size depends on the learner's existing knowledge
Encoding, storage, and retrieval; retrieval cues and encoding specificity; retrieval as an event that changes memory
Schemas as organized knowledge in long-term memory, and schema acquisition and automation as the goal of instruction in cognitive load theory
Cognitive load theory: intrinsic load from element interactivity relative to expertise, extraneous load from presentation, and the changed status of germane load
Well-replicated instructional implications: retrieval practice (quizzing) and spaced practice, with the IES practice guide evidence ratings
The learning-styles meshing hypothesis and why the evidence does not support it
supporting: The multicomponent working memory model as the successor to the modal model's short-term store
The unresolved argument about whether short-term storage is a separate store or activated long-term memory
The Cepeda et al. finding that the optimal interstudy interval grows with the intended retention interval
Deep explanatory questions as a second strongly rated recommendation in the same federal guide
Judgments of learning and the mismatch between fluency and durable learning
outOfScope: Behaviorism beyond a brief contrast (separate topic in this unit, already written)
Constructivism and social learning theory (separate topics in this unit)
Neuroscience of memory consolidation, hippocampal systems, and memory disorders
Clinical or diagnostic guidance about working memory deficits in an individual student
Full treatment of metacognition and self-regulated learning
Piagetian stage theory (covered under cognitive development)

claims.claim: Cognitive science took shape in the 1950s out of psychology, linguistics, anthropology, computer science, and neuroscience, and psychology's break from behaviorism was what made cognition scientifically respectable again.

The modal model of Atkinson and Shiffrin describes memory as sensory registers feeding a limited short-term store that feeds a long-term store, with control processes such as rehearsal moving information between them; the short-term store concept developed into the multicomponent working memory model.

Whether short-term storage is a distinct store or simply activated long-term memory is still argued; Baddeley, Hitch, and Allen review recent proposals to replace the short-term store with activated long-term memory and question them.

Miller (1956) argued that the span of immediate memory is roughly seven items and is almost independent of how much information each item carries, that it is a different limitation from the span of absolute judgment, and that recoding material into fewer, larger chunks is how people get past the limit.

Current estimates put the core capacity of working memory at roughly three to five chunks in young adults, commonly summarized as three or four, observed under conditions that prevent rehearsal, grouping, and other strategies; Cowan reports that adults recall only three or four longer verbal chunks such as idioms or short sentences, and only three or four pre-existing chunks when strategies are unavailable.

Chunking is the formation or recognition of associations that reduce the number of independent items to be held, so chunk size depends on what the learner already knows; the educational implication Cowan draws is to adjust materials to the working memory the learner has rather than trying to enlarge capacity.

Memory is usefully analyzed as encoding, storage, and retrieval; retrieval success depends on cues, and cues work best when they match the conditions of encoding (encoding specificity), while a cue linked to too many memories loses its power (cue overload).

Roediger and Karpicke (2006) found that repeated studying beat repeated testing on a final test given five minutes later, but prior testing produced substantially greater retention on final tests given two days or one week later.

In the 2007 IES practice guide, the panel rated using quizzes to re-expose students to key content as supported by strong evidence, spacing learning over time as moderate, interleaving worked example solutions with problem solving as moderate, asking deep explanatory questions as strong, and pre-questions, delayed judgments of learning, and using tests to identify content needing study as low.

The meta-analysis by Cepeda and colleagues located 839 assessments of distributed practice in 317 experiments in 184 articles and concluded that interstudy interval and retention interval act jointly, with the interval producing maximum retention increasing as the retention interval increases.

Cognitive load theory rests on the architecture that novel information is first processed by a working memory limited in capacity and duration and then stored in an effectively unlimited long-term memory for later use.

Intrinsic cognitive load comes from the inherent complexity of the material, indexed by element interactivity and relative to the learner's expertise; extraneous cognitive load comes from how the material is presented and is the part instructional design controls.

Germane load is no longer treated as an independent, additive third source of cognitive load; Kirschner, Sweller, Kirschner, and Zambrano work with intrinsic and extraneous load only, cite Kalyuga's argument that germane load is essentially indistinguishable from intrinsic load, and note that germane load retains a use only if redefined as the working memory resources actually devoted to dealing with intrinsic rather than extraneous load.

Validating learning-styles-based instruction requires a specific experimental result: students grouped by learning style, randomly assigned to instructional methods, given the same final test, producing a crossover interaction in which the best method differs by group. Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer, and Bjork found virtually no evidence of that pattern, noted that several studies using an appropriate method flatly contradicted the meshing hypothesis, and concluded there is no adequate evidence base for putting learning-styles assessments into general educational practice.

A direct test following that design found no statistically significant relationship between auditory or visual-word learning-style preference and either verbal comprehension aptitude (listening versus reading) or comprehension after instruction by digital audiobook versus e-text, on immediate or two-week delayed tests.

The same review reports that people do express consistent preferences about how information is presented and that people differ in aptitudes for processing different kinds of material; what fails is the inference that instruction should be matched to those preferences.
Learning and memory reconstruct knowledge rather than replaying stored copies, and what a learner recalls is shaped by prior knowledge and by the retrieval cues available in the environment.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many chunks working memory holds
positions: Miller (1956): the span of immediate memory is about seven chunks, largely independent of the information per chunk.
Cowan (2010, 2014): the core capacity is about three to four chunks when rehearsal, grouping, and long-term memory strategies are prevented; higher spans reflect those supplementary strategies.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches Miller's claim as the historically important one and Cowan's as the current estimate, and makes the boundary conditions explicit rather than swapping one slogan for another. It also states plainly that a chunk is not a fixed unit, so any capacity number is a number of chunks, not of facts.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The status of germane cognitive load
positions: Early cognitive load theory treated germane load as a third, additive source of load that instruction should increase.
Kalyuga argued germane load is essentially indistinguishable from intrinsic load and therefore redundant.

Kirschner, Sweller, Kirschner, and Zambrano (2018) work with intrinsic and extraneous load only, and allow germane load a role only if redefined as the working memory resources devoted to dealing with intrinsic rather than extraneous load.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the two-source account, names germane load as a term that changed meaning, and explicitly warns against the still-common textbook advice to 'increase germane load' as though it were a third dial.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether short-term storage is a separate store
positions: The modal model and the multicomponent working memory model posit dedicated short-term storage.
Some researchers propose replacing short-term storage with activated long-term memory; Baddeley, Hitch, and Allen review and question those proposals.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Reported as an open theoretical argument. The lesson uses the functional facts (severe capacity limit, dependence on prior knowledge) that hold under either account.

positions: Roediger and Karpicke (2006): repeated studying beat repeated testing at a five-minute delay.
The same experiments: testing beat studying at two days and one week.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the reversal rather than the headline, and uses it to teach that immediate performance is a poor proxy for durable learning.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How completely learning styles have been refuted
positions: Pashler et al. found virtually no support for the meshing hypothesis and several contradicting results from studies with adequate designs.
The same authors caution that most versions of the learning-styles idea have simply never been tested, so it would be an error to say all of them have been tested and found wanting.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the correction firmly (there is no adequate evidence base for matching instruction to styles) while keeping the authors' own caveat about untested variants, and adds the Rogowsky et al. direct test as a concrete negative result.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive factual claims about cognitivism at all; its body text was placeholder prose about defining a concept and applying it to an example.
The draft's Eli-10 analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer') carried no explanatory content about memory or processing and had no statement of where the analogy fails.
The draft's three quick-check items tested generic study advice rather than any cognitivist idea, and had three options each rather than four.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire placeholder lesson with sourced content on the information-processing model, capacity limits, chunking, encoding and retrieval, schemas, and cognitive load theory.
Added the required correction of the learning-styles meshing hypothesis, with the experimental criterion that would be needed to support it and two sources showing it is not met.
Treated germane load carefully rather than repeating the older three-load formulation, because Sweller and colleagues no longer treat it as an independent additive source of load.
Stated Miller's seven-plus-or-minus-two as a historical claim and gave the current three-to-four-chunk estimate with its boundary conditions.
Reported the IES practice guide's actual recommendation-by-recommendation evidence ratings, verified against the published guide, rather than describing the whole guide as strong evidence.
Kept behaviorism and constructivism out of scope except as brief contrasts, and used behaviorism terminology consistent with the already-published behaviorism lesson.
rightsIssues: No source prose was reproduced or paraphrase-followed. All lesson wording is original.
The Noba module is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; NonCommercial and ShareAlike terms were not cleared for this project, so it is recorded as reference only.
Kirschner et al. (2018) is CC BY 4.0 and would permit reuse with attribution, but no wording was reused; it is recorded as attribution-required for accuracy.
The IES practice guide is a federal report whose reuse terms were not separately verified, so it is recorded as reference only, consistent with the behaviorism topic's treatment of WWC guides.

Journal articles from Psychological Science, Psychological Bulletin, Psychological Science in the Public Interest, Journal of Educational Psychology, Memory and Cognition, Current Directions, Educational Psychology Review, and Trends in Cognitive Sciences are reference only; facts were synthesized from abstracts, author manuscripts, or author-posted copies.

sourceRecords.provider: Pashler, H. (chair), Bain, P., Bottge, B., Graesser, A., Koedinger, K., McDaniel, M., Metcalfe, J.; National Center for Education Research, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education
sourceRecords.notes: Federal practice guide used for the recommendation-level evidence ratings, verified against the full guide text (Table 2 and the per-recommendation 'Level of evidence' statements): spacing moderate; interleaving worked examples with problem solving moderate; combining graphics with verbal descriptions moderate; connecting abstract and concrete representations moderate; 5a pre-questions low; 5b quizzes to re-expose students to key content strong (nine K-12 experiments, more than 30 college experiments, plus a large laboratory literature); 6a delayed judgments of learning low; 6b using tests to identify content needing study low; 7 deep explanatory questions strong. sourceRecords.title: The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information (Psychological Review, 63, 81-97)
sourceRecords.provider: George A. Miller; hosted by Classics in the History of Psychology, York University
sourceRecords.notes: Primary source for the seven-plus-or-minus-two claim, for Miller's insistence that the span of immediate memory is measured in chunks rather than bits, for his distinction between the span of absolute judgment and the span of immediate memory, and for recoding as the way to get more information into a fixed number of chunks. Reuse terms for the 1956 article were not verified, so it is recorded as reference only and no wording was reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: The Magical Mystery Four: How Is Working Memory Capacity Limited, and Why? (Current Directions in Psychological Science, 19(1), 51-57)
sourceRecords.provider: Nelson Cowan; NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC2864034)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the revised capacity estimate of three to five chunks in young adults, for the finding that adults recall only three or four longer verbal chunks such as idioms or short sentences, and for the experimental conditions needed to observe the core limit (blocking rehearsal with articulatory suppression, brief simultaneous arrays, unattended channels, running-span procedures, masking of sensory memory).

sourceRecords.title: Working Memory Underpins Cognitive Development, Learning, and Education (Educational Psychology Review, 26(2), 197-223)
sourceRecords.provider: Nelson Cowan; NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC4207727)
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the definition of chunking as forming or recognizing associations that reduce the number of independent items, for the point that chunk size depends on prior knowledge, and for the instructional conclusion that materials should be adjusted to the learner's existing working memory rather than attempting to expand capacity.

sourceRecords.title: From short-term store to multicomponent working memory: The role of the modal model (Memory and Cognition, 47(4), 575-588)
sourceRecords.provider: Alan D. Baddeley, Graham J. Hitch, Richard J. Allen; author accepted manuscript, White Rose Research Online
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the description of the Atkinson and Shiffrin modal model and its components, for the development of the short-term store concept into the multicomponent working memory framework, and for the fact that proposals to replace short-term storage with activated long-term memory are current and contested.

sourceRecords.title: From cognitive load theory to collaborative cognitive load theory (International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 13(2), 213-233)
sourceRecords.provider: Paul A. Kirschner, John Sweller, Femke Kirschner, Jimmy Zambrano R.; PubMed Central (PMC6435105)
sourceRecords.license: CC BY 4.0 (as stated on the article page)
sourceRecords.notes: Open-access paper co-authored by Sweller, used for the current two-source account of cognitive load: intrinsic load as the inherent complexity of the information determined by element interactivity and learner expertise, extraneous load as the load imposed by presentation, and germane load as no longer an independent additive source - citing Kalyuga's argument that it is indistinguishable from intrinsic load, and allowing it only if redefined as the working memory resources devoted to dealing with intrinsic rather than extraneous load. Facts synthesized; no wording reused.

sourceRecords.title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later (Educational Psychology Review, 31(2), 261-292)
sourceRecords.provider: John Sweller, Jeroen J. G. van Merrienboer, Fred Paas; ERIC record EJ1217401
sourceRecords.notes: Used for the architectural premise of cognitive load theory - that novel information is first processed by a working memory limited in capacity and duration and then stored in an effectively unlimited long-term memory for later use - and for the point that instructional design long proceeded without reference to those structures. Abstract-level verification only; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence (Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9(3), 105-119)
sourceRecords.provider: Harold Pashler, Mark McDaniel, Doug Rohrer, Robert Bjork; author-posted copy, Bjork Learning and Forgetting Lab, UCLA
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read for the definition of the meshing hypothesis, the four experimental criteria the authors require (grouping by learning style, random assignment to methods, a common achievement test, and a crossover interaction), the finding of virtually no evidence for that interaction, the observation that several studies using an adequate method flatly contradicted the meshing hypothesis, the conclusion that there is no adequate evidence base for incorporating learning-styles assessments into general educational practice, and the authors' own caveat that many versions of the idea have never been tested.
